entries: Sir Isaac Newton (1643–1727) was an English scientist who gave the laws of motion and universal gravitation, co-invented calculus, and explained that white light is made of colours.
Albert Einstein (1879–1955) was a German-born physicist who developed the theory of relativity (E = mc²) and explained the photoelectric effect, for which he won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) was an Italian astronomer and physicist who improved the telescope, discovered Jupiter's four largest moons, and supported the idea that Earth goes around the Sun. He's called the father of modern science.
Charles Darwin (1809–1882) was an English naturalist who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection in 'On the Origin of Species' (1859), after studying animals on the Galápagos Islands.

Nikola Tesla (1856–1943) was an inventor who developed the alternating current (AC) electricity system, the induction motor and many ideas behind radio and wireless power. The SI unit of magnetic flux density, the tesla, is named after him.

Michael Faraday (1791–1867) was an English scientist who discovered electromagnetic induction, which made electric generators and transformers possible. The farad, the unit of capacitance, is named after him.

Stephen Hawking (1942–2018) was a British physicist famous for his work on black holes (Hawking radiation) and his book 'A Brief History of Time'. He lived with motor neurone disease for over 50 years.
Ada Lovelace (1815–1852) wrote what is considered the first computer program, for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, so she's called the first computer programmer.

Alan Turing (1912–1954) was a British mathematician who founded computer science with the idea of the Turing machine, helped break the German Enigma code in World War II, and proposed the Turing test for AI.
Bill Gates (born 1955) co-founded Microsoft with Paul Allen in 1975, which made the Windows operating system and Office. He later focused on charity through the Gates Foundation.
Steve Jobs (1955–2011) co-founded Apple with Steve Wozniak in 1976 and led the creation of the Macintosh, iPod, iPhone and iPad.
Google was founded by Larry Page and Sergey Brin in 1998, when they were PhD students at Stanford University. Sundar Pichai, born in Madurai, Tamil Nadu, became Google's CEO in 2015.
Facebook (now Meta) was founded by Mark Zuckerberg and his college roommates at Harvard in 2004.
Amazon was founded by Jeff Bezos in 1994 as an online bookstore; it grew into one of the world's largest companies, including Amazon Web Services (AWS).
Elon Musk (born 1971) is an entrepreneur who leads SpaceX (rockets and Starlink) and Tesla (electric cars), and co-founded PayPal.
Homi J. Bhabha (1909–1966) was the father of India's nuclear programme and founded TIFR (Tata Institute of Fundamental Research) and the Atomic Energy Establishment, later renamed BARC.
Who was Srinivasa Ramanujan's teacher at Cambridge?
G. H. Hardy, the English mathematician, invited Ramanujan to Trinity College, Cambridge in 1914 and worked with him. Hardy called their partnership the one romantic incident in his life.
Sir Jagadish Chandra Bose (1858–1937) was an Indian scientist who pioneered radio and microwave research and showed that plants respond to stimuli, using his crescograph.
Satyendra Nath Bose (1894–1974) was an Indian physicist who, with Einstein, developed Bose–Einstein statistics. Particles called bosons are named after him.
Vikram Sarabhai (1919–1971) is the father of India's space programme: he founded ISRO in 1969 and the Physical Research Laboratory.
M. S. Swaminathan (1925–2023), born in Kumbakonam, Tamil Nadu, was the agricultural scientist who led India's Green Revolution, introducing high-yield wheat and rice varieties.
Verghese Kurien (1921–2012), the 'Milkman of India', led Operation Flood — the White Revolution — that made India the world's largest milk producer, and built Amul.

A. R. Rahman (born 1967 in Chennai) is a music composer called the 'Mozart of Madras'. He won two Oscars and a Grammy for 'Slumdog Millionaire' (2009), and composed for Roja, Bombay and many more films.
Ilaiyaraaja (born 1943) is the legendary Tamil film composer called 'Isaignani', who has composed over 7,000 songs for more than 1,000 films and a symphony.
Rajinikanth (born 1950) is a hugely popular Tamil film actor, known as 'Superstar', famous for his style in films like Baasha, Padayappa, Sivaji and Enthiran. He received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award.
Kamal Haasan (born 1954) is an acclaimed Tamil actor, director and writer called 'Ulaganayagan', known for films like Nayakan, Anbe Sivam and Vishwaroopam.

M. G. Ramachandran (MGR, 1917–1987) was a hugely popular Tamil film actor who founded the AIADMK party and was Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu from 1977 to 1987. He brought in the nutritious noon meal scheme.
C. N. Annadurai (Anna, 1909–1969) founded the DMK party and became Chief Minister in 1967. He renamed Madras State as Tamil Nadu in 1969.
E. V. Ramasamy (Periyar, 1879–1973) was a social reformer who led the Self-Respect Movement against caste discrimination and for women's rights and rational thinking.
Sachin Tendulkar made the most runs in both Test and ODI cricket, and was the first to score 100 international centuries and the first to score a double century in an ODI (2010).

M. S. Dhoni (born 1981) is a former Indian cricket captain, the only captain to win all three major ICC trophies: the T20 World Cup (2007), the ODI World Cup (2011) and the Champions Trophy (2013). He's called 'Captain Cool'.
Virat Kohli (born 1988) is an Indian batter who has scored the most centuries in ODI cricket (passing Sachin Tendulkar's 49 in 2023) and captained India in all formats.
P. T. Usha, the 'Payyoli Express', is India's legendary sprinter who finished fourth in the 400 m hurdles at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, missing a medal by 1/100 of a second.
Mary Kom from Manipur is a six-time World Amateur Boxing Champion and won bronze at the 2012 London Olympics.
P. V. Sindhu is an Indian badminton player who won silver at the 2016 Rio Olympics and bronze at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, and became world champion in 2019.
Milkha Singh (1929–2021), the 'Flying Sikh', was India's great sprinter who won gold at the 1958 Commonwealth Games and came fourth in the 400 m at the 1960 Rome Olympics.
Cristiano Ronaldo (born 1985) is a Portuguese footballer, one of the greatest ever, and the all-time top goalscorer in men's international football.
Lionel Messi (born 1987) is an Argentine footballer who has won a record eight Ballon d'Or awards and led Argentina to win the 2022 FIFA World Cup.
Pelé (1940–2022) was a Brazilian footballer who won three FIFA World Cups (1958, 1962, 1970), the only player to do so.
Usain Bolt from Jamaica is the fastest sprinter ever: he holds the world records for 100 m (9.58 s) and 200 m (19.19 s), set in 2009, and won eight Olympic gold medals.
Michael Jordan (born 1963) is an American basketball legend who won six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls.
Mother Teresa (1910–1997) was a nun who served the poorest people in Kolkata through the Missionaries of Charity. She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and the Bharat Ratna in 1980.
Winston Churchill (1874–1965) was the British Prime Minister who led Britain through most of World War II. He also won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953.

Adolf Hitler (1889–1945) was the Nazi dictator of Germany from 1933 to 1945 who started World War II in Europe and was responsible for the Holocaust, the murder of six million Jews and millions of others.
Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) was an Italian Renaissance genius: painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and an inventor, engineer and anatomist.
William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was an English playwright and poet, often called the greatest writer in English. His plays include Hamlet, Romeo and Juliet, Macbeth, Othello and King Lear.

Gautama Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama), born in Lumbini around the 5th–6th century BCE, founded Buddhism. He gained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya and taught the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.
Vardhamana Mahavira was the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism, who taught ahimsa (non-violence), truth and non-attachment.
Guru Nanak (1469–1539) founded Sikhism and was the first of the ten Sikh Gurus. His teachings are in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Who was Raja Ram Mohan Roy?
Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1772–1833), the 'Father of the Indian Renaissance', founded the Brahmo Samaj and campaigned successfully against sati.
Savitribai Phule (1831–1897) was India's first woman teacher; with her husband Jyotirao Phule she opened one of the first schools for girls in Pune in 1848.

Sarojini Naidu (1879–1949), the 'Nightingale of India', was a poet and freedom fighter, the first woman president of the Indian National Congress (1925) and the first woman governor of an Indian state.
Lal Bahadur Shastri (1904–1966) was India's second Prime Minister, who gave the slogan 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan'.
Bal Gangadhar Tilak (1856–1920) was a freedom fighter called 'Lokmanya', who declared 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it!'
Chanakya (Kautilya), about the 4th century BCE, was the teacher and adviser of Chandragupta Maurya and wrote the Arthashastra, a book on statecraft and economics.
